This vase's shape and decoration are typical of the Art Nouveau period,
hence its title. However, if you like the shape but not the surface, decorate
yours in your signature style to make it unique to you

a cone shape, barely dampen the surface of the batt
and position it at the centre.

DECORATING YOUR VASE
Our decorating method incorporated the Cuerda Seca
method of decoration.
Cuerda Seca means 'dry cord' in Spanish and is an
ancient technique for creating line decoration on a
ceramic surface using a mixture of wax emulsion and
a colourant to keep the glaze colours separated. It's a
technique that adds wonderfully graphic definition to
drawings but does take some practice to perfect.
Cuerda Seca wax recipe:
• Liquid wax emulsion 50g
1 Standard borax frit 3g
• Red iron oxide 5g
• Black iron oxide 5g
Method of mixing:
Wet the oxides thoroughly in a few drops of water, then
mix them into the wax.
Pass the mixture through an 80-mesh sieve to remove
any lumps - transfer the mixture to a suitable container
that can be kept airtight.
Immediately wash the sieve in boiling water and
washing-up liquid.
Note: Make only a small amount to begin with; it will
be enough for you to try out the technique to see if you
like it.

• If you want to decorate your vase in an Art Nouveau
style, do some research to find images that suit the
vase's shape or could be adapted accordingly.
You can stick imagery into your sketchbook if you
want to or draw the designs in as you prefer.
When you have decided on an image you like, scale
it up to fit the proportions of your vase in a repeat of at
least three around the outer surface.
A Transfer the design to a sheet of tracing paper using
a good graphite pencil (or carbon paper), then holding
the tracing paper firmly on the side of the vase, transfer
the design to the surface.
• Using the Cuerda Seca wax emulsion and a fine
brush, carefully work over the drawn outline of the
design on the vase.
When the Cuerda Seca has dried, paint the design
in your chosen colours of glaze, applying as many
layers as recommended by the manufacturer to
complete the vase.
Remember to include the interior and
background in the design.

RECYCLING CLAY AND
GLAZE MATERIALS
Linda Bloomfield is a scientist
turned potter. More glaze
recipes can be found in her
books, Advanced Pottery (2011),
Colour in Glazes (A&C Black
2012), The Handbook of Glaze
Recipes (Bloomsbury 2014)
and Science for Potters (The
American Ceramic Society 2017).
Her new book Special Effect
Glazes, and the second edition
of Colour in Glazes are both out
now. Linda has recently launched
her online glazing course, How
Glazes Work, on her website:
lindabloomfield.co.uk
Turning a porcelain bowl. The turnings can be recycled.
R
cycling is something that
we can all do to help make
pottery more sustainable.
As well as re-using
packaging materials for sending
pottery, it is also a good idea to recycle
some of the materials we use for
making pottery.
Studio potters might worry that the
materials they use, clays and glaze
ingredients, are mined from the earth
and are not renewable. However, with
the exception of pure, white kaolin, clay
is very common worldwide, the result
of weathering and crumbling of
mountains, the residue deposited in
rivers and lakes over millions of years,
part of the geological cycle which could
be seen as long-term, natural recycling.
Even so, clay bodies can be expensive,
particularly porcelain, so it is a good
idea to recycle all your waste clay in the
studio. When recycling ceramics, the
clay and glaze waste need to be
separated. If this is not done, the fluxes
in the glaze may cause the recycled clay
to warp and slump during firing. It is
also a good idea to collect different
coloured clay waste in separate
containers and recycle them separately,
particularly if you use both
earthenware and stoneware clays that
are fired to different temperatures.
Alternatively, you could use the
recycled mix of clays for projects where
the colour is not so important, for
example, anything you intend to cover
with a dark or opaque glaze.
You can recycle all unfired clay.
Collect together failed pots, throwing
slurry, trimmings and turnings. It is
important to add the throwing slurry,
which contains the finest clay particles,
essential for good plasticity of the clay.
If you have thrown the slurry away, add
a small amount (a teaspoon) of
bentonite mixed with water to improve
the plasticity. If everything is still in
the wet state, wedge it together by
combining it into a large mass, cutting
it in half and slamming the two halves
together repeatedly until the texture
becomes homogenous. If the clay has
gone beyond leather hard, dry out until
completely bone dry and then add to
water to allow to slake down, leave to
settle, then pour off excess water and
dry out the slurry on a plaster batt to a

MUGS, CUPS, BEAKERS, EGG CUPS
Mug's can be cylindrical, conical (either tapered or flared
towards the rim) or a more rounded, bellied shape. The
rim is very important; it should be fine, smooth and feel
good to drink from. A slightly turned out rim is easier
to drink from than one that is turned in. The rim can be
bevelled to make it thinner at the outer edge of the wall
but not so thin that it will chip easily; the rim needs to
be rounded, with a radius on the edge, rather than too
angular and sharp. Modern mugs need to be big enough
to hold a cup of tea or coffee and often have boiling
water poured in straight from the kettle so new clay/
glaze combinations should be tested for thermal shock; a
mismatch in thermal expansion between the glaze and
clay body can cause cracking.

MIXING CLAYS TO MAKE A SUITABLE
BODY
Before you begin:
The method of firing we are advising on here
places a significant strain on the clay used to
construct the forms, so we must begin with
choosing the right clays. Attention to detail
when making the forms will also pay dividends
to successfully get them through the firing
CLAY
Your clay supplier will be able to advise you on
suitable clays for extreme firings like smoke and
raku. Most have an excellent selection, with
some made specifically for this type of work
- Ashraf Hanna's body being one. However, the
general principle is that the clay needs to have
an open body that incorporates a good amount
of grog. There are many you could try, Crank
and T-Material are particularly good choices,
but the latter can be very expensive. The
exception to the rule is porcelain, which
generally fires really well in this way. It should
be said that, as with all aspects of working with
clay, it is a matter of trial and error, and testing
different clays is strongly advised.
The colour of the clay is another
consideration, and for the best colour response
in the fired form, a white or pale body is always
a good option. No matter the mix of clays (or
not, if you're using a commercially prepared
one), some will need to be refined to make a
slip to fit the body exactly, for burnishing. If the

mix is already white-firing, it can be coloured

A favourite body for smoke firing is one I
make myself from a mixture of T-Material and

T-Material is made from a blend of low-

perfect clay for extreme firing processes

shock and is suitable for hand building to any
The fired colour is light but greyish, so adding
porcelain whitens and refines it.
For a pinkish body, you could replace the
porcelain with a red clay, like smooth
terracotta, or you could mix porcelain with a
crank body etc. The most important element of
deciding on a clay body is that you can work
with it easily and that it will withstand the firing
method.

applied to the form's surface before burnishing,

USING THE TOOLS
Burnishing is a slow and methodical business that is
either meditative or laborious, depending on how
you feel!
There is no hard and fast method; the aim is to
compact the surface by repeatedly rubbing over it
until the surface is smooth and shiny.
The surface must be leather hard to burnish
successfully, so begin by working over it in a circular
action or from side to side, using your chosen tools
- you will need more than one if there are difficult
angles on your form.
Continue until the surface is smooth and shiny.
Finally, work over it with the rib held at a flat angle to
cover a wide area.
Bisque-fire burnished vessels to no higher than
1000°C but preferably around 960°C to maintain the
burnished shine.
Note: The surface will lose the burnished effect if
bisque-fired too high, although it will remain smooth.

2023 is the centenary year of
Michael Cardew joining Bernard
Leach and Shoji Hamada in St Ives
as the first apprentice at the Leach
Pottery. Cardew was an
extraordinary potter whose work I
greatly admire. We own quite a few
of his early slipware pots, including
the one in the photo that I picked up
a few weeks ago, which was made at
Winchcombe Pottery following his
apprenticeship. Of all studio potters,
he is (except for my wife, of course)
my greatest influence.
We're greatly honoured to have
been invited to present a solo
exhibition at the Leach Pottery in
February as part of the Cardew
Centenary Celebrations. The Leach
Pottery is where the British Studio
Pottery Movement began, so it's
important to us. As ever, we're
going to need to burn the midnight
oil to make it happen, but we will,
and I look forward to making some

is infuriating. Everything takes so
much longer to do than I expect it
to. At least there's plenty to look
forward to.

enjoy some invaluable family time
away from the workshop, even if our
heads and conversations will still be
filled with pottery.
